query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Under prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures combined with cyclic mechanical loading, an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy develops nanoscale precipitates at its grain boundaries that coalesce into a continuous network. This network acts as a stress concentrator and promotes intergranular crack initiation, leading to a transition from ductile to brittle behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with a uniform elemental distribution and no pre-existing grain-boundary precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled thermal aging (e.g., 500–600°C) together with cyclic mechanical loading that simulates long-term service conditions.
generation.conditions: Aging durations and cyclic loading amplitudes designed to mimic realistic service environments; tests conducted in a controlled atmosphere to minimize extrinsic effects (e.g., oxidation).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and evolution of nanoscale precipitates at grain boundaries—from an initially discontinuous dispersion (e.g., ~5 nm thick) to a continuous intergranular film (e.g., ~19 nm thick).
generation.mechanism: Thermal aging increases atomic mobility, especially along grain boundaries, while cyclic loading amplifies local strain. This combination accelerates the nucleation, growth, and interconnection of precipitates at grain boundaries, which serve as sites of local stress concentration and ultimately trigger a brittle failure mode.
generation.predicted_outcome: After aging and cyclic loading, the precipitate volume fraction at grain boundaries will increase, with a transition toward a continuous network. This will manifest as a marked reduction in ductility and fracture toughness (e.g., lower tensile ductility and earlier intergranular fracture) compared to the as-cast alloy.
generation.baseline: The as-cast single-phase alloy exhibits ductile, transgranular failure with no significant precipitate formation at grain boundaries under similar mechanical loading but without aging-induced microstructural evolution.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate under long-term service conditions involving moderately high temperatures (500–600°C) combined with repeated mechanical stress. Under static, isothermal conditions or at temperatures well outside this range, the same evolution may not occur.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature-duration thresholds and loading parameters necessary to induce the precipitate network transition are not fully defined and may vary with minor compositional fluctuations and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nominally identical single-phase high-entropy alloy samples. Expose one set to controlled thermal aging within the 500–600°C range combined with cyclic mechanical loading that simulates long-term service conditions, while keeping a control set under static conditions (or minimal service-like cyclic loading). After treatment, perform detailed microstructural analysis (using TEM/SEM) to assess precipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution along grain boundaries and conduct mechanical tests (tensile and fracture toughness) to evaluate toughness degradation.
measurements: Grain-boundary precipitate size and continuity (via TEM/SEM imaging)
Precipitate volume fraction at grain boundaries
Fracture surface characterization (to distinguish intergranular vs transgranular failure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in grain-boundary precipitate connectivity (i.e., no transition from discontinuous to continuous precipitate networks) and if mechanical testing does not reveal a notable reduction in toughness (ductility and fracture toughness remain comparable to the control), the hypothesis that precipitation-induced embrittlement governs toughness degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ). cited_evidence.text: The presence and characteristics of precipitates play a crucial role in determining the mechanical properties of MPEAs, particularly in terms of strength and ductility. In this study, precipitates were observed to significantly influence the mechanical properties of both HF1 and HF2 alloys, with a direct correlation between precipitate formation and strength enhancement, as well as a trade-off with ductility. In the case of the HF1 alloy, precipitates formed at the grain boundaries upon aging at 500 °C for 30 min, leading to an increase in strength from 971 MPa to 1081 MPa.
